result: PNab is a pan-neuronal antibody that stains all nerve cells in Hydra. Validation experiments using three transgenic lines (alpha-tubulin, Hym176B, nGreen) showed 100% co-localization of transgenic nerve cells with PNab staining (684/684, 149/149, 51/51 respectively). Both maceration and confocal imaging yielded identical nerve cell to epithelial cell ratios of 0.12.
evaluation: Claims C13, C22-C25 provide strong convergent evidence from multiple independent validation approaches. The 100% co-staining across three different transgenic lines and the concordance between two independent counting methods (maceration and confocal imaging) robustly support that PNab is a reliable pan-neuronal marker.

result: Hydra possesses two anatomically separate nerve nets, one in the ectoderm and one in the endoderm, with no connections between them. Systematic imaging of tissue rings from four animals containing 133 nerve cells revealed no contacts between the ectodermal and endodermal nerve nets.
evaluation: Claims C14, C16, and C28 are supported by systematic confocal imaging data. The quantitative analysis of 133 nerve cells across 4% of body column tissue from four animals provides substantial evidence for the absence of connections, though the sample represents a limited portion of total tissue.

result: The distribution of nerve cells varies dramatically along the body axis. The endoderm of tentacles completely lacks nerve cells, while the basal disk has very few endodermal nerve cells. The endodermal nerve cell density is relatively constant (0.10-0.19) in the body column, while ectodermal nerve cell density is constant (0.15-0.22) in the gastric region and peduncle but increases sharply in the hypostome, tentacles, and basal disk.
evaluation: Claims C17, C29-C33 are supported by quantitative cell counting data from confocal imaging (Figure 6) and confirmed by historical observations. The absence of endodermal nerve cells in tentacles is particularly striking and well-documented. However, the manuscript notes the results are semi-quantitative with variable numbers of animals scored at different positions.

result: The nerve nets consist of discrete bundles of overlapping neurites rather than simple end-to-end connections. In the ectoderm, ~80% of nerve tracks occur as bundles of 2-5 neurites, with only ~20% as single neurites. In the endoderm, ~50% are single neurites and ~50% are bundles of two neurites, with no bundles containing more than two neurites.
evaluation: Claims C15, C34-C38 are supported by convergent evidence from confocal microscopy (Figure 7), TEM cross-sections (Figure 9), and 3D block face SEM reconstruction (Figure 10). The quantitative analysis of bundle composition from TEM provides robust structural data, though the sample size for TEM analysis is limited to specific tissue regions.

result: The ectodermal nerve net is more directly associated with muscle processes and exhibits higher connectivity than the endodermal nerve net.
evaluation: Claims C39-C40 are supported by both confocal imaging (Figure 4) and TEM data (Figure 9) showing the spatial relationship between nerve cells and muscle processes, as well as quantitative bundle analysis demonstrating greater complexity in the ectoderm. The convergent anatomical and quantitative evidence strongly supports this conclusion.

result: Different neural circuits express distinct innexins that can form circuit-specific gap junctions. The CB circuit (ec1/ec5) expresses innexin 2, the RP1 circuit (ec3) expresses innexins 6 and 14, and the RP2 circuit (en1) expresses innexin 2. Gap junctions between neurites in bundles were observed by TEM.
evaluation: Claims C19, C46-C48, C93-C94 are supported by scRNAseq data (Figure 12C) showing differential innexin expression and TEM images showing gap junctions (Figure 12A-B). The inference that circuit-specific gap junctions provide specificity is logical given the anatomical evidence of mixed circuits in bundles (Figure 11) and the expression data, though direct functional validation is not provided.

result: The nerve net grows by lateral addition of new nerve cells to existing neurite bundles. Grafting experiments tracking newly differentiated nerve cells showed that most cells without neurites on day 1 were not associated with the nerve net, but by days 2-3, most differentiating nerve cells extended neurites along the existing nerve net.
evaluation: Claims C20-C21, C50-C52 are supported by grafting experiments with quantitative tracking data (Figure 13). The temporal progression of neurite association with the nerve net provides strong evidence for the lateral addition model. The structural observations of neurite bundles (C34-C38) provide independent support for this growth mechanism.

result: The RP2 neural circuit corresponds to the endodermal nerve net identified by PNab staining, with no RP2 nerve cells in tentacles. The CB network activity correlates with rapid body column contraction, while RP1 and RP2 networks associate with slower behavioral changes.
evaluation: Claims C54-C57 integrate anatomical data from the current study with neural activity data from Dupre and Yuste, 2017. The correspondence between anatomical localization (PNab staining) and functional circuits (GCaMP6s activity) is well-supported by the concordance of observations, particularly the absence of endodermal nerve cells in tentacles matching the absence of RP2 activity there.

result: During fast body column contraction initiated by CB nerve cells, both ectodermal and endodermal epithelial cells respond simultaneously despite the absence of neural connections between the two layers. This suggests ectodermal epitheliomuscle cells activate endodermal epitheliomuscle cells directly via gap junctions across the mesoglea. The ectodermal nerve net has direct contacts with muscle processes, while such contacts are rare in the endoderm.
evaluation: Claims C58-C61 integrate findings from multiple studies. The anatomical observations from the current study (C60-C61) are well-supported by TEM and confocal data. The inference about gap junction-mediated communication (C59) is logical given the simultaneous activation without neural connections, though it relies on cited work rather than direct demonstration in this manuscript.

result: The endodermal nerve net functions in regulating digestion and osmotic pressure control. Endodermal sensory cells (>50% of endodermal nerve cells) extend cilia into the gastric cavity to monitor digestive activity. Endodermal ganglion cells (N4) regulate mouth opening in response to body column swelling, and their ablation prevents mouth opening and delays food pellet expulsion. The absence of endodermal nerve cells in tentacles is consistent with tentacles not being involved in digestion.
evaluation: Claims C69-C74, C76-C77 are supported by anatomical observations (C70-C71) from the current study and functional data from cited work (Giez et al., 2023a). The inference about endodermal nerve net function (C69) is well-supported by convergent evidence from nerve-free animals and ablation experiments. Claim C71 includes speculation about osmotic sensing that is not directly tested.

result: Nerve cells in the endoderm are removed when endodermal tissue moves into tentacles, likely by apoptosis, though this has not been observed directly.
evaluation: Claim C84 is a logical inference from the observation that body column endoderm contains nerve cells but tentacle endoderm does not. However, the mechanism (C85) is speculative and acknowledged as not directly observed. Alternative mechanisms for nerve cell removal have not been ruled out.

result: Although PNab was made against a peptide in H. vulgaris cadherin, it does not recognize the cadherin protein. The antibody peptide sequence is not conserved in H. oligactis and H. viridissima cadherins, yet PNab stains neurons in all three species. The identity of the PNab antigen is unknown, but PNab is a highly specific pan-neuronal marker across Hydra species.
evaluation: Claims C86-C92 are supported by sequence alignment data (Figure 15) and cross-species validation. The logic is sound: if PNab recognized cadherin, it should not stain neurons in species lacking the peptide sequence. The specificity of PNab as a pan-neuronal marker is well-established by the validation experiments (C22-C25), even though the actual antigen remains unidentified.

result: Background on Hydra nervous system: 500-2000 nerve cells depending on size; two morphological types (ganglion and sensory cells) with no glial cells; ganglion cells are bipolar/multipolar without axon-dendrite distinction; sensory cells are polarized with cilia extending to external surface (ectoderm) or gastric cavity (endoderm); scRNAseq refined classification to three sensory and five ganglion populations.
evaluation: Claims C1-C9 are background information supported by multiple citations to prior work. These are well-established facts about Hydra nervous system organization that provide context for the current study.

result: Hydra tissues, including the nerve net, are continuously renewed every 2-3 weeks in well-fed animals. Cell proliferation occurs exclusively in the body column, with continuous displacement toward head and foot. Tentacle tissue is renewed in 4-5 days. Nerve cell differentiation occurs throughout the body column and maintains constant nerve to epithelial cell ratios.
evaluation: Claims C10-C12, C78 describe the dynamic nature of Hydra tissue turnover, supported by citations to prior work and data from the current study (Figure 6). This provides important context for understanding nerve net growth and maintenance.

result: Nerve cell bodies are roughly 10 μm long, with variable spacing between cell bodies (usually 50-100 μm) in both ectoderm and endoderm. The distance between nerve cell bodies in the 3D reconstruction is roughly 50 μm, consistent with confocal observations.
evaluation: Claims C26-C27, C41 provide quantitative morphological measurements from confocal imaging and 3D reconstruction. The consistency between different imaging modalities supports these measurements, though they represent descriptive rather than mechanistic findings.

result: Based on the Hydra single cell atlas, there is one ganglion nerve cell population in the endoderm (en1, corresponding to RP2 circuit) and two populations in the ectoderm (ec1/ec5 and ec3, corresponding to CB and RP1 circuits).
evaluation: Claims C42-C45 are supported by citations to the Hydra single cell atlas and neural activity studies. These provide the molecular and functional context for interpreting the anatomical observations in the current study.

result: Endodermal ganglion cells express neuropeptides including GLWa, which induces slow endodermal contraction and body column elongation. Ectodermal circuits express distinct neuropeptides: ec1/ec1/5 express Hym176, while ec3 cells express GLWa.
evaluation: Claims C62-C65 are supported by citations to scRNAseq data and functional studies. This provides molecular characterization of the different neural circuits identified anatomically in the current study.

result: Nerve-free Hydra no longer contract and are nearly motionless due to absence of ectodermal nerve cells. The body column is distended by osmotic pressure that cannot be released through the closed mouth, but experimental mouth opening restores normal morphology.
evaluation: Claims C66-C68 are supported by citations to studies of nerve-free animals. This provides functional context for understanding the role of the nerve nets, particularly the ectodermal net in motor control and the endodermal net in osmotic regulation.

result: During digestion, slow waves of radial contraction move along the oral/aboral axis mixing gut contents. Following prey ingestion, endodermal muscle processes below the tentacle ring contract locally (neck formation) while body column muscles relax, creating a closed space for digestion. After digestion, slow endodermal muscle contraction restores normal body column form.
evaluation: Claims C75, C100-C102 describe digestive behaviors supported by citations to prior work. These provide functional context for understanding the role of the endodermal nerve net in regulating digestion.

result: The existing nerve net acts as a template for the addition of new nerve cells.
evaluation: Claim C79 is an inference supported by the structural observations of neurite bundles and the grafting experiments showing lateral addition. This represents a conceptual model that integrates multiple lines of evidence from the study.

result: Specialized neural populations exist in specific body regions: a fourth GCaMP6s activity pattern at the tentacle base associated with head nodding; Nv1 sensory cells incorporated into battery cell complexes in tentacle ectoderm; innexin2-expressing nerve cells in the lower peduncle whose gap junction activity is required for normal body column contractile activity.
evaluation: Claims C80-C83 are supported by citations to prior work characterizing region-specific neural populations. These provide examples of functional specialization within the nerve nets.

result: Evolutionary context: nerve cells arose early in multicellular animal evolution to sense the environment and control effector cells. In non-bilaterians (cnidarians and ctenophores), nerve cells are organized in nerve nets associated with muscle processes. In bilaterians, nerves are organized into centralized nervous systems with large ganglia.
evaluation: Claims C95-C97 provide evolutionary context supported by citations to prior work. This frames the significance of studying the Hydra nerve net as a model for understanding early nervous system organization.

result: Hydra polyps live in fresh water with constant water influx into epithelial cells. This water is transferred to the gastric cavity and periodically voided through the mouth and potentially through the basal disc pore.
evaluation: Claims C98-C99 describe basic Hydra physiology supported by citations. This provides context for understanding osmotic regulation as a function of the endodermal nerve net.

result: Elimination of nerve cells leads to polyps that do not move and are incapable of capturing and ingesting prey.
evaluation: Claim C53 is supported by citation to Campbell, 1976, establishing the functional importance of the nerve net for behavior. This provides motivation for the detailed anatomical characterization in the current study.

result: There is no cross-correlation between the neural activity profiles of CB and RP2 and RP1 and RP2, indicating that the endodermal and ectodermal neural circuits are not connected.
evaluation: Claim C49 is supported by citation to neural activity measurements by Dupre and Yuste, 2017. This functional evidence independently supports the anatomical observation of no connections between ectodermal and endodermal nerve nets.
